newsitem.title: CONGO: Brazzaville government bans private militias.
newsitem.headline: Brazzaville government bans private militias.

text.p: The Congolese government on Friday banned private militias and the unauthorised bearing of arms following renewed clashes in the north of the country ahead of July's presidential election.
A government decree limited the maximum security detachment of former heads of state to 30 soldiers, and that of ex-ministers, deputies and other senior officials to two.

Twelve people were killed between May 7 and 11 in clashes between supporters of former president Denis Sassou Nguesso and former prime minister Jacques Joachim Yhombi-Opango in the town of Owando, 600 km north of the capital.

Sassou Nguesso, beaten by incumbent president Pascal Lissouba in the 1992 elections, is in the north as part of an undeclared campaign for the presidential polls. He has not yet officially said he will run.
Yhombi-Opango, a former general who was head of state before Sassou-Ngessou, is from the Owando region.
About a dozen candidates are expected to contest the elections. The three front-runners are Lissouba, Sassou Nguesso and Bernard Kolelas, 1992 runner-up and mayor of Brazzaville.

On Thursday, security forces killed one man and wounded another who were among a gang of five armed men trying to set fire to the homes of Yhombi-Opango, Owando's mayor, and a local parliamentary deputy, state radio reported.
Political militias were officially dissolved following a peace accord in 1995 but have continued to operate discreetly.

Followers of Lissouba and his ruling Panafrican Union for Social Democracy (UPADS) are known as "Zulus", followers of Kolelas and his Congolese Movement for Democracy and Integral Development (MCDDI) call themselves "Ninjas", and followers of Sassou Nguessou and his Congolese Labour Party (PCT), the former single party, are known as "Cobras".

The militias were formed during ethnic and political fighting in Brazzaville in 1993 which killed 2,000. The ban has been welcomed by Congolese fearing renewed violence in the run-up to July's presidential election, but is likely to be difficult to implement in practice.

Congo is also housing growing numbers of mainly Rwandan Hutu refugees fleeing former Zaire following Laurent Kabila's takeover. The Brazzaville government is keen to repatriate them as soon as possible.
